PADUCAH, Kentucky (CNN) -- The aunt of former U.S. soldier Steven Green told jurors tearfully Monday that "We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq" as defense lawyers worked to save her nephew from a death sentence. Former U.S. soldier Steven Green has been convicted of raping and killing a 14-year-old Iraqi girl. Patty Ruth, a Texas elementary school principal, told a civilian jury about Green's childhood as a reader who loved to be hugged by relatives. "I do not know how we got to this spot," Ruth said in emotional testimony. "I do not know how this happened." Green was convicted last week in U.S. District Court in Kentucky of murder, rape, conspiracy and obstruction of justice in connection with a 2006 rape-and-murder south of Baghdad. A jury found him guilty of raping a 14-year-old girl, then killing her and setting her body on fire to destroy evidence. Green also was found guilty of killing the girl's parents and 6-year-old sister. He could become the first former U.S. soldier to face the death penalty for war crimes before a civilian court, where he was tried because he had been discharged from the military before his crimes came to light. Four other former soldiers are in prison for their roles in the crimes and the cover-up that followed. Green faces either death or life in prison without the possibility of parole. His fate will be in the hands of the jury by week's end. The defense has presented relatives and medical professionals who have pieced together a picture of Green's childhood as troubled and stressful. It included the breakup of his parents' marriage, routine beatings to the point of injury by an older brother and being moved about through Texas by his mother. Ruth, the final witness scheduled by the defense, said that when the idea of the military came up for her nephew, she was unsure the Army would accept him. Even after he received a high school diploma through a correspondence course, she said, "I could not picture or imagine how he could make it through basic training." Ruth said when she saw a picture of her nephew before his September 2005 deployment, she knew he wasn't "Stevie" anymore, standing as tall as his father in the photo at Fort Benning, Georgia. When he returned from Iraq 11 months later, he was "remarkably thin," Ruth said, and she noticed circles under his eyes. Green and his father spent a night at the Ruth home, his aunt said, and she remembered him pacing the yard while smoking. He fell asleep wearing his fatigues, she said. When asked by the defense about the rape-murder plot that left an Iraqi family dead near Yusufiya, about 20 miles south of Baghdad, Ruth responded, "He's my Steve. You can't stop loving someone." There were other family members in the court on Monday. Green's father, John, an oil field worker from Midland, Texas, looked on quietly. He did not testify. Ruth, who is John Green's sister, noted for the jury that Green's mother is not at the trial this week. The mother is moving and had to attend a going-away party, Ruth said. Final arguments are expected Wednesday.

# Jury Deliberates Fate of Former Soldier Convicted in Iraqi Family's Murder as Aunt Delivers Tearful Testimony

*By CNN Staff*

**PADUCAH, Kentucky** — The sentencing phase of the federal trial against Steven Dale Green, the former U.S. Army soldier convicted of raping and murdering a 14-year-old Iraqi girl and killing three members of her family, entered an emotional new stage this week as prosecutors and defense attorneys presented dueling portraits of the man now facing a possible death sentence.

Green, 24, was found guilty earlier this month on all 17 counts related to the 2006 killings in Mahmudiyah, Iraq, an attack that shocked the nation and became one of the most notorious war crimes cases to emerge from the Iraq conflict. Prosecutors say Green and several fellow soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division plotted the assault while off duty, ultimately raping 14-year-old Abeer Qassim Hamza al-Janabi before killing her, her parents, and her young sister, then attempting to burn the bodies to conceal the crime.

Because Green had already been discharged from the Army when the crimes came to light, he was tried in federal civilian court rather than by military tribunal — a decision that placed the death penalty back on the table in a case that has drawn international scrutiny.

## A Family Divided by Grief

The most striking moment of the week came Wednesday, when Green's aunt, Dorothy Green Cummings, took the stand as a defense witness, offering a raw and often tearful account of her nephew's troubled childhood in an effort to persuade jurors to spare his life.

"He was not born this way," Cummings told the courtroom, her voice breaking as she described a home marked by instability, addiction, and neglect. "Nobody reached out. Nobody asked what was happening to that little boy behind closed doors."

Cummings described a chaotic upbringing in Midland, Texas, recounting instances of domestic violence she said Green witnessed as a young child, as well as periods when he was left largely unsupervised. She testified that Green had once shown promise — "a sweet boy who loved animals and wanted, more than anything, to be a soldier" — before what she described as a slow unraveling that neither she nor other relatives recognized in time.

"I keep asking myself what I could have done," she said, pausing repeatedly to compose herself. "I loved him. I still love him. But I cannot make sense of what happened to that family, and neither can he."

At one point, Cummings turned toward the gallery, where relatives of the victims sat in silence, and offered a halting apology on behalf of her family. "There are no words," she said. "There will never be words big enough."

Several jurors appeared visibly moved during the testimony; one wiped away tears as Cummings described visiting Green in jail in the months after his arrest and finding him, in her words, "a shell of the boy I remembered."

## Prosecution Pushes Back

Prosecutors, however, argued that Green's difficult childhood does not diminish the calculated brutality of the crime. Lead prosecutor Marisa Ford reminded jurors during cross-examination of Cummings that Green had, according to trial testimony, boasted about the killings to fellow soldiers in the days afterward, describing the attack in graphic detail with apparent lack of remorse.

"This was not a moment of madness," Ford told jurors in closing remarks for the day. "This was planned. This was premeditated. And this family — this innocent Iraqi family — paid the price for it."

Family members of Abeer al-Janabi, some of whom traveled from Iraq to attend the proceedings, have sat through the sentencing phase largely without speaking to reporters, their attorneys citing the emotional toll of reliving the crime in open court.

## What Comes Next

The jury, which convicted Green on charges including conspiracy to commit aggravated sexual assault, rape, and murder, must now decide whether he will be sentenced to death or to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Deliberations are expected to resume Monday after the defense concludes its mitigation case, which is expected to include additional testimony from mental health experts regarding Green's psychological state at the time of the killings.

Legal analysts following the trial say the case remains a landmark test of how the American justice system handles atrocities committed by service members abroad, and note that a death sentence would make Green one of the few U.S. soldiers in modern history executed for crimes committed during wartime deployment.

CNN will continue to follow developments in the sentencing phase as they unfold.
